text: Sir Alec John Jeffreys, CH FRS MAE (born 9 January 1950), is a British geneticist renowned for developing techniques for genetic fingerprinting and DNA profiling, which are now used worldwide in forensic science to assist police detective work and to resolve paternity and immigration disputes. He is professor of genetics at the University of Leicester and became an honorary freeman of the City of Leicester on 26 November 1992. In 1994, he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to genetics. Born into a middle-class family in Oxford, Jeffreys spent his first six years there before moving to Luton, Bedfordshire in 1956. He attributes his curiosity and inventiveness to his father and paternal grandfather, who held patents. At age eight, his father gave him a chemistry set, which he enhanced with extra chemicals, including a small bottle of sulphuric acid; an accidental splash caused a burn that left a permanent scar on his chin (now under his beard). His father also bought him a Victorian-era brass microscope, which he used to examine biological specimens. At about 12, he made a small dissecting kit, including a scalpel crafted from a flattened pin, to dissect a bumblebee, and later a deceased cat he found on the road while doing his paper round; dissecting the cat caused a foul smell when he ruptured its intestines. Jeffreys attended Luton Grammar School and Luton Sixth Form College, winning a scholarship to study at the University of Oxford’s Merton College, where he graduated in 1971 with first-class honours in biochemistry. He completed his Doctor of Philosophy degree on the mitochondria of cultured mammalian cells in the genetics laboratory. After his doctorate, he worked as a research fellow at the University of Amsterdam before joining the University of Leicester in 1977, where in 1984 he discovered a method of showing variations between individuals' DNA, inventing and developing genetic fingerprinting. He had a "eureka moment" in his lab on 10 September 1984 after observing an X-ray film of a DNA experiment that unexpectedly showed both similarities and differences between family members' DNA, realizing the potential of DNA fingerprinting to identify individuals. The method is now used in forensic science, paternity testing, and immigration disputes, and can also be applied to non-human species. Before commercialization in 1987, his laboratory was the only center in the world conducting DNA fingerprinting and received global inquiries. In 1985, his method was first used in a disputed immigration case to confirm the identity of a British boy from Ghana, whose DNA proved close relation to the family, bringing relief to the mother. DNA fingerprinting was first used in a police forensic case to identify the killer of Lynda Mann and Dawn Ashworth, murdered in 1983 and 1986 respectively in Narborough, Leicestershire; Colin Pitchfork was identified and convicted after DNA matches from his semen samples, and Richard Buckland, initially a suspect, was exonerated. The case is detailed in Joseph Wambaugh's 1989 book The Blooding and featured in Episode 4 of the 1996 American TV series Medical Detectives, with a further mini-series released in 2015 titled Code of a Killer. In 1992, Jeffreys' methods were used by German prosecutors to confirm the identity of Josef Mengele, who died in 1979, by comparing DNA from a femur bone of his exhumed skeleton with DNA from his mother and son, similar to paternity testing. DNA profiling, based on typing individual highly variable minisatellites in the human genome, was developed by Jeffreys and his team in 1985, with the term "DNA fingerprinting" retained for the initial test that types many minisatellites simultaneously. By focusing on a few highly variable minisatellites, DNA profiling became more sensitive, reproducible, and suitable for computer databases, becoming the standard forensic DNA system globally. The development of DNA amplification via the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) enabled automation, increased sensitivity, and the use of alternative marker systems. The most commonly used markers are now variable microsatellites, or short tandem repeats (STRs), which Jeffreys first exploited in 1990 in the Mengele case. STR profiling was refined by Peter Gill’s team at the Forensic Science Service in the 1990s, leading to the launch of the UK National DNA Database (NDNAD) in 1995. With automated and sophisticated equipment, modern DNA profiling can process hundreds of samples daily. The current NDNAD system uses sixteen microsatellites plus a sex determination marker, providing a discrimination power of one in over a billion. Under British law, anyone arrested in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland has their DNA profile taken and stored in the database, regardless of conviction (different rules apply in Scotland). As of 2020, the national database contained DNA information from about 5.6 million people. Jeffreys has opposed the current use of DNA profiling with government access to the database and has proposed a database of all people's DNA, with access controlled by an independent third party. His former doctoral students include Turi King. Jeffreys met his future wife, Sue Miles, in a youth club in central Luton before becoming a university student and married her on 28 August 1971. He has one brother and one sister and two daughters, born in 1979 and 1983.
